— How much of your free time is spent indoors? Supervised by a parent or other adult?

URBANA, ILL. — The crime is known as the
grandparent scam
. It’s a type of identity theft that many people have been aware of for a while, but my grandfather had not heard about it before he fell prey to it.
A few years ago, a young woman pretending to be me called my grandfather on his landline and asked him to bail her out of a situation she had become embroiled in while traveling in Spain. Drugs were involved, a lost passport, the police, and the caller pleaded with my grandfather not to alert my parents to her troubles. She began to cry and my grandfather promptly gave in to her demands. Over about a day and a half, he sent three wire transfers totaling a little under $6,000 to a Western Union office in Spain.
I learned all of this about a week and a half later, when my grandfather called me and asked, sounding both hurt and surprised, “When did you get home?”
I initially thought he was referring to a trip I’d made to New York the previous month, and I told him that it had been a couple of weeks since my return.
“No,” he said. “When did you get home from Spain?”
My stomach shifted queasily. “I wasn’t in Spain,” I said.
He told me then about the girl, about how her voice had sounded so much like mine. He did not want to believe that he had been conned. The girl and her accomplices must have looked me up online and learned enough details about my family and career to convincingly impersonate me. She knew my mother’s and stepfather’s names, a detail that still chills me. Where had she found them? But then I remembered — there was a short essay on my website about my parents’ dog, and I must have mentioned their names in it.
“She sure sounded like you,” my grandfather said. “She started crying and, well, I was sure it was you, Christine.”
I was horrified and incredulous. But above all, I was furious.
“Grandpa,” I said. “I’m so sorry, but it wasn’t me. I think this was a scam. Did you really wire her some money?”
He laughed again, embarrassed. “Three different times,” he said. “They got me for some collect calls, too.”
“You need to call the police right away,” I said.
He was quiet, thinking this over. “The girl was so convincing. She gave me a number for a police officer and when I called it, he confirmed the girl’s story.”
“That’s all part of the scam,” I said. “They’re organized. They’ve done it many times.”
I asked if he had talked to my uncle Cory, who oversees his finances. I thought that it was important for Cory to know what had happened.
My grandfather agreed to contact the police but did not want to call my uncle. More than having his money stolen, he worried about losing his autonomy, I later learned from his sister. He was 86 then, and feared that my uncle or another family member would deem him incapable of caring for himself and pack him off to a nursing home. I knew that wasn’t likely to happen (and it hasn’t), but I didn’t fully understand the intensity or the cause of my grandfather’s anxiety before I disobeyed him and called Cory myself.
Cory was upset that my grandfather had been robbed and thought that the incident had most likely hurt his pride, but he reassured me that my grandfather had always been frugal, and that the money he’d lost would not lead to any hardship. I offered to pay back in installments the money he had lost. But he hasn’t accepted it. He insists that he was responsible, that it was his mistake and he should be the one to pay for it.
I thought of my grandfather again a few weeks ago, when my partner’s debit card number was stolen, and his checking account drained in about 20 minutes. Being the victim of a crime feels aggressively personal. It is a reminder of our essential vulnerability — the feeling of exposure is what we find most difficult to recover from.
After hours spent on the phone and at his local bank, my partner eventually got his money back. My grandfather never did.
Since that day when my grandfather called to ask if I had returned from Spain, we have spoken to each other only two more times. We have always kept in touch, mostly through handwritten letters, but his arrive infrequently now. Each time I’ve tried to call him, he has hung up. Despite what he has told me, I worry that he is angry with me, for embarrassing him, for calling my uncle. One afternoon, I called three times, trying to convince him that it really was me, and not someone pretending to be me. He hung up on me twice; the third call went to voice mail. I believe he’s afraid that his ears are again deceiving him. I can clearly picture him on the other end of the line, but I don’t know how to reach him.
Christine Sneed
is the author of the forthcoming novel “Paris, He Said.”

A funny thing happened in the waiting room of a suburban Maryland car repair place the other day. We were all minding our own business, looking at the screens of our mobile devices, until the local news on a television there aired a story that united a group of strangers.
It turns out the staff members and customers of that repair shop had a fair amount in common: We’d all been children, we were all parents, and we were all horrified by the
sanctioning
of two fellow Maryland parents for the crime of
letting their kids (10 and 6 years old) walk home alone from the park
.
Danielle and Alexander Meitiv were found responsible for “unsubstantiated child neglect” after a two-month investigation by Montgomery County Child Protective Services. As far as the waiting room could tell, the finding means the Child Protective Services will keep a file on the family for many years. It also seems that the family could face repercussions if they do anything to catch Child Protective Services’ attention, like letting their children walk unaccompanied again.
Everyone in the waiting room started talking. We told stories. The estimator said he couldn’t have been more than 7 or 8 when he and an older friend rode their bikes all the way from suburban Maryland to the zoo in Washington. It must have been nearly 10 miles each way. The rest of us nodded in understanding. Back in the 1970s and ’80s, we’d disappear for hours as children. The front desk person said she used to climb trees and read for hours in the branches, unnoticed, content. My friends and I went through a phase where we’d go around collecting neighborhood road kill, burying our dead squirrels and birds with solemn funerals.
Someone raised the subject of our own children. I recalled how my son described a recent snowstorm as one of the best days of his life. He and friends were outside for four hours; they jumped creeks, built forts, sledded, threw snowballs. It seemed as if everyone in the room had a snow story; we had a good time with those.
And then one of the men offered a different kind of story. He’d been a single parent raising his son, and he couldn’t afford child care. So from a pretty early age (the legal limit in Maryland) his boy got himself home from school, let himself in the apartment, and waited until his dad came home. He smiled then, at the memory of his boy. “He wasn’t lonely, though, he was always outside, playing with his friends.” Then the guy shook his head. “What would they do to me now if they saw him out there playing? Would they try to take him?”
It’s not an absurd question. A South Carolina mother was arrested last summer for
leaving her child at a nearby park
while she was at work. She also could not afford child care.
I don’t mean to scapegoat child service workers, who were no doubt just following their rules. But we need to recognize that well-intended laws aimed at protecting vulnerable children from real abuse and neglect can have unintended consequences, and one of those consequences is that parents will believe that letting kids be kids — the kinds of kids they themselves often were — will put their family in danger, even if the children themselves are at statistically little risk of anything but poor choices.  (That stuff still gets back to parents via phone calls, texts and informative neighborhood list-serves — the latter, in fact, is how I heard that some of the snowball throwing that was part of my son’s excellent day was not appreciated by all our neighborhood drivers. The children won’t do that again.)
My new waiting room acquaintances and I agreed that parents should be able to send their children to the park to play without fear from the authorities, just as our parents used to do. To us children of the 1970s and ’80s, it’s feeling a little personal. It’s starting to seem as if someone’s saying the way we were raised is no longer O.K. And speaking for a lot of us, we disagree. We liked our way.
I’ve been sensing a healthy backlash against the kind of helicopter parenting that smothers a child and doesn’t let him or her grow, learn from their mistakes, even figure out how to be bored.  Unfortunately, while more and more parents seem to want to just say no to excessive hand-holding, that’s clearly not the case with all our bureaucracies. As one fellow parent noted, looking wistfully out the repair shop window at the snow-covered landscape, “It’s almost like they’d rather our kids sit in the basement and play video games for hours than wander outside.”
Here in Maryland, it does kind of feel like that. And if feels wrong.

The actor talks to Taffy Brodesser-Akner about steamy “X-Files” fan fiction and his new novel, not suitable for Disney.
You have a novel coming out, “Holy Cow,” about a traumatized cow, a sassy turkey and a pig converting to Judaism. What was the impetus to write a book like this?
Ten years ago I had this idea come to me: If I were a cow, why wouldn’t I try to get to India? So I wrote up a treatment, and I pitched it to the only places you can pitch it, Disney and Pixar. Obviously they were wise to stay away from a story that has a pig getting circumcised in it. And then one day last year, I just thought, Well, why don’t I write out that idea?
It’s a very Jewish story. The pig in the book, Shalom, fixes the Israel-Palestine conflict. Your father was Jewish and your mother is Lutheran. How were you raised?
I was raised in New York City. I was raised on the streets. I went to a Presbyterian school. I wasn’t raised to believe in any particular god. My father was a kind of cultural Jew, I’d say. So if I have a Jewish sensibility, I think it’s more in the cultural sense.
Your character on “Californication” is a novelist. How would he blurb “Holy Cow”?
He would’ve said, “I don’t blurb, and I don’t like using blurb as a verb.”
You majored in English at Princeton, and your thesis was called “The Schizophrenic Critique of Pure Reason in Beckett’s Early Novels.” What?
You know what the alternative title for that is? “David Duchovny Is an Arrogant Idiot.”
What is it about?
Exactly. Let me try to remember. I think I was under the sway of some French Lacanian literary critics, Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari. To put it as simply as I can, the paper posed the question: Why is everybody striving to be a Freudian neurotic when that, actually, could be the biggest sickness of all?
Your novel also critiques industrial agriculture. Are you still a vegetarian?
I’m a very lazy vegetarian, which means I will look for the vegetarian meal, but I will also give up. I don’t think I eat red meat anymore. Let’s say no, I don’t. I’ll eat fish. I hear insects are going to be the next source of protein, and I look forward to that. I’m O.K. with killing insects.
I’m O.K. with killing them, too. I’m less sure about eating them.
What I like about insects is they enjoy horrible living conditions and filth, unlike mammals. They do. That’s what they live in. I have no problem with them living in teeming, overcrowded feces-filled environments. That’s where they want to be.
Your former “X-Files” co-star, Gillian Anderson, recently published her first novel, too. So, in a sense, did Agents Scully and Mulder end up together after all?
No. I think it’s very rare to have two writers in the household. Isn’t it? There was a rumor a couple of years ago that we were living together.
There is a lot of Mulder-Scully fan fiction, and some of it is pretty “Red Shoe Diaries,” if you know what I mean.
You’re using all my work against me. When “X-Files” was kind of in its heyday, that was the beginning of the Internet. I was very skeptical and thought, This thing will never last. My favorite was the fan fiction that had Alex Krycek, my nemesis, and me as lovers. It was beautiful.
Do you think of your work as being in the tradition of Samuel Beckett or are you more of a Gillian Anderson?
I didn’t read Gillian’s book. We just had breakfast a few days ago, and she didn’t even mention that she had one. I didn’t know. But no, I still like language a little too much to call myself Beckettian. He is very austere, and I like fooling around with words. I guess I’m more Joycean, although that’ll sound
really
pretentious.
Do conspiracy theorists still seek you out?
It’s been a while since somebody tried to get me information that just had to get out. I have received some letters about abductions in my day that were sad and interesting.
Are there any episodes of “The X-Files” that haunt you in particular?
Oh, no, no, just my acting in some of the early ones affects me to this day. I wish that they would be destroyed.

who spent most of his adult life in New York City
, was particularly adept at capturing the alienation, but also the beauty, of big city living.
One of his most famous paintings,
“Early Sunday Morning, Seventh Avenue,”
occupies a prime spot in the Whitney’s new installation of its permanent collection,
“America Is Hard to See.”
The painting shows a row of small brick buildings, washed in sunlight, facing a deserted street.
It’s almost like a stage before the curtains have risen, and the actors taken their place.
